sec1.lens: This is a positioning session disguised as a prework checklist — Fountainhead is asking 'whose source are you?' and the Godfather Offer is asking 'what would be impossible to say no to?' — both questions collapse if the dream customer is fuzzy.
emphasis: Push on WHO specifically cannot refuse the Godfather Offer — not 'entrepreneurs' or 'coaches,' but a named human with a named problem at a named moment
Force the client to articulate what 'source' they're the head of in ONE sentence — if they can't, they don't have a Fountainhead yet, they have a puddle
Drag the mentor list out of abstraction — 'whose work do you steal nothing from but honor everything of?' — the answer reveals the lineage their offer sits inside
common_traps: Listing generic mentors (Tony Robbins, Brendon Burchard) instead of the three people whose specific moves they've actually absorbed into their teaching
Writing the Fountainhead definition as a mission statement instead of a source-of-stream claim — 'I help people heal' is not a Fountainhead, 'I'm the source of the breath-first approach to X' is
Skipping the prework videos and pretending they get it — then building a Godfather Offer that's just a course with two PDFs taped to it
voice_notes: Who is the ONE person — first name, age, last Tuesday night crisis — who sees this offer and physically cannot click away?
If your dream customer's best friend had to describe your work in one sentence at a dinner party, what would they say? If that sentence is boring, the Fountainhead isn't there yet.
A Godfather Offer isn't a bundle. It's a moment where the math stops making sense in the buyer's favor. Where does your stack break their calculator?

sec2.lens: The 4 Levels Of Value pyramid is beautiful theory, but 'Level 10 Opportunity' only becomes real when it's anchored to a specific human transformation — otherwise it's a vision-board exercise.
emphasis: Push past 'platform' fantasy — Russell built ClickFunnels because he had spent YEARS doing the Level 3 Communication work; if the client hasn't done that work, their Level 10 is a daydream
Ask for the ONE person whose life their Level 10 changes — abstract 'people I'm called to serve' is a red flag, specific 'Maria, 47, teacher in Ohio' is gold
Pressure-test the skill self-scores — most people rate themselves a 7 on communication when they're actually a 4; ask them to show me their last three sales pages or emails
common_traps: Scoring themselves 8/10 on communication because they 'talk well,' when communication in Russell's frame means 'I can write a webinar that converts cold traffic' — very different skill
Jumping to Level 4 Imagination without ever having mastered Level 3 Communication — you can't skip the Mouth to get to the Mind
Writing a Level 10 Opportunity that's really just 'make more money doing what I already do' — that's not a Level 10, that's a raise
voice_notes: Russell went from 3 to 200 million dollars not because he had a better idea, but because he changed WHO the idea was for. Who is your Level 10 idea for?
The 4 Levels aren't a ladder you climb — they're a diagnostic. Where does YOUR money actually come from right now? Be honest. Not where you wish it came from.
If your Level 10 Opportunity doesn't scare you a little, it's not a 10. It's probably a 6 with a nice font.

sec3.lens: This is the single most important conceptual pivot in the whole workbook — Improvement vs. New Opportunity is the engagement-or-dead-scroll moment, and most clients will try to fake it by renaming their improvement offer.
emphasis: Hunt down the 'repackaged improvement' — if the client's new opportunity is 'a better version of what they already tried,' it's still improvement, just with a new hat

Push on the 'old vehicle' question until they can name the ACTUAL vehicle their dream customer is currently driving — 'another course' isn't specific enough, 'the 12-week group coaching program they bought last October that didn't work' is
Demand 8 real arguments for why THIS is the only way — most people stop at 3 and wave their hands; the grind of arguments 5-8 is where the irresistible hook lives
common_traps: Claiming a 'new opportunity' that's really just their old method with new branding — the test is whether the dream customer would describe it as 'like X but better' (improvement) or 'something I've never heard of before' (new opportunity)
Writing 'new discovery' as the driver when the thing isn't actually new to the market — Napoleon Hill's information business was genuinely novel; 'my 5-step framework' is not
Mistaking the vehicle for the destination — your dream customer doesn't want your method, they want the result your method delivers. Keep naming the result.
voice_notes: Your dream customer has a receipt in their drawer from the last three times they tried to fix this. Why is YOUR thing not going to end up as receipt number four?
'New opportunity' doesn't mean new to the WORLD. It means new to THEM. What have they genuinely never seen before — in a way they'd feel in their body?

Here's the test: can you describe your opportunity in one sentence where the listener says 'wait, what?' — if they say 'oh, like that other thing,' you've got an improvement offer and you're going to lose.

sec4.lens: The Stack Slide is the most mechanically useful page in the entire workbook — but the 10:1 value ratio only works if every stack item is something the dream customer would actually pay for separately; inflated fantasy values kill trust faster than low prices.
emphasis: Ruthlessly audit each stack item — 'would a cold visitor pay this dollar amount for this one thing alone?' — if no, the number is fiction and the whole stack smells like a car dealership

Push for complementary, not redundant — 4-6 items that each solve a DIFFERENT failure point in the buyer's journey; if three of them teach the same thing, it's not a stack, it's a stack of the same pancake
Force the 'already have' audit first — clients routinely overlook assets they've built (past webinars, Q&A recordings, PDFs from old launches) that are stack gold with zero new creation work
Drill the Priceless bonus — what's the emotional, identity-level inclusion that can't be priced? That's the one that actually closes.
common_traps: Slapping $997 on a PDF because the template says so — the value has to be DEFENSIBLE if the buyer asks 'where does this number come from?' — if you can't answer, the number breaks the room
Stacking things the buyer doesn't actually want (checklists, cheatsheets, 'swipe files') to hit a big number — six boring items is worse than three great items
Forgetting that the stack is a PROMISE of transformation, not a pile of assets — each item needs a line describing the shift it produces, not just the format it comes in
Building the stack before they know who the dream customer is — you can't stack value for a ghost
voice_notes: Every item on your stack has to pass the 'at 2 AM' test — if your dream customer is staring at this slide at 2 AM with their credit card on the desk, does THIS specific item tip them over? If not, cut it.
The Priceless bonus is not a gimmick. It's the thing that says 'I see you, and I'm giving you something that money can't actually buy.' What's yours?
Your total value isn't a sum. It's a story. Each line is a chapter in the story of 'how we're going to get you there.' Does your stack read like a story or like a receipt?
Stop building Frankenstein stacks. Four items that belong together beats seven items that you Velcroed on to hit a number.

sec5.lens: This is a preview section doing exactly what a preview should do — tease the Curiosity Headline and 3 Secrets while confirming the Offer is locked — but it's intentionally thin, so I'm not going to score it like it's a teaching module.
emphasis: Push the client to draft a rough Curiosity Headline NOW — not to finalize, but to see what their brain produces before Module 2 structures them (the first instinct often reveals the real hook)
Have them pre-guess their 3 Secrets — the guess is usually wrong, but comparing their guess to what comes out of Module 2 shows where their blind spots live
Make the marketplace browsing an actual exercise, not a box-check — 'find 3 funnels that make you feel something and tell me WHY' is the real assignment
common_traps: Treating the preview as 'just a preview' and skipping it — the prework is where the subconscious starts cooking on Module 2's problems
Browsing the marketplace passively instead of dissecting specific funnels — scrolling is not research
Writing a 'curiosity headline' that's actually just a value proposition ('Learn how to X') — curiosity lives in INCOMPLETE information; a clean promise is not a hook
voice_notes: Your Curiosity Headline isn't a promise. It's a DOOR. It has to be the kind of door someone HAS to open because they can't stand not knowing what's behind it.
If your headline could work for any course in your niche, it's not a headline — it's a category label. Keep going.
The 3 Secrets aren't tips. They're the three things your dream customer believes right now that are keeping them stuck — and the three things you're going to replace those beliefs with.
